text: François-Alexandre Verdier won the Prix de Rome for drawing in 1668 with a piece called Première conquête de la Franche-Comté. He won it again in 1671 for Le Roi donnant la paix à l'Europe. He studied under Charles Le Brun and worked as his assistant. For a few years he lived at the Medici Villa in Italy. The Academy admitted him in 1678. Many of his drawings and paintings are in the Louvre.

Gustave Boulanger's first picture sent home from Rome, Phryné, disappointed the Academy and scandalised critics. He had been orphaned at 14, and his uncle sent him to study with Paul Delaroche, where he befriended Jean-Léon Gérôme. The two became leading lights of the Néo-Grec movement. Boulanger won the Prix de Rome in 1849 with Ulysse reconnu par Euryclée and stayed in Italy until 1855, studying the excavations at Pompeii and travelling to Greece. Later he managed Gérôme's studio at the École des Beaux-Arts whenever Gérôme went east.

Lattanzio Gambara was fifteen when he apprenticed with Giulio Campi in Cremona. By 1549 he was working alongside Girolamo Romanino, who became his father-in-law. He painted frescoes in the Villa Contarini in Asolo. A fresco cycle on the History of the Apocalypse in the Loggia of Brescia was destroyed by bombing in 1944. Later he went back to Brescia to work with Romanino on frescoes for Sant'Eufemia and Saint Lorenzo, most of them now lost. In 1565 he worked briefly in Venice.

Peter von Hess joined General Wrede's staff during the Napoleonic Wars and painted his first battle pieces there. He had trained with his father and with Wilhelm von Kobell, and he followed his younger brother Heinrich Maria to Munich in 1806. In 1818 he painted Italian landscapes and scenes and travelled to Naples with a group of Bavarian artists. In 1833 King Ludwig I asked him to accompany Otto of Greece to Athens, where he gathered material for pictures of the war of liberation. Forty of his sketches ended up in the Pinakothek.

Charles-Dominique-Joseph Eisen became drawing-master to Madame de Pompadour. He was born in Valenciennes, the son and pupil of Frans Eisen, and entered Le Bas's studio in Paris. His wit won him a place at court as painter and draftsman to the King. He is best known for book illustrations and vignettes, among them the plates for the Fermiers généraux edition of La Fontaine's Contes. Later he fell into disgrace. In 1777 he retired to Brussels, where he died in poverty.

Cornelis Ketel wanted to paint history, but neither England nor Holland had a market for it, so he became a portraitist. Born in Gouda, he worked at Fontainebleau in 1566 and had to leave France the next year, when all citizens of the Habsburg Netherlands were expelled. He painted at the Tudor court in the 1570s and married in London in 1573. Back in Amsterdam he introduced the full-length group portrait to the Dutch burghers with great success. He was also a poet and orator, and from 1595 a sculptor.

Dirk van Lokhorst spent his whole life in Utrecht. He specialised in landscapes and animals and studied under the cattle painter Albertus Verhoesen and Johannes Bilders. He also worked as a portrait photographer. He set up a lithographic factory in Utrecht and added a photographic facility in 1860, and he was probably one of the first in the Netherlands to make photo lithographs. His pupils included his son Dirk Pieter and the marine painter Jacob Eduard van Heemskerck van Beest.

Christian Friedrich Zincke came to London in 1706 to work in Charles Boit's studio. When Boit left for France eight years later, Zincke inherited many of his fashionable clients. He went on to become the most successful enamel painter of his era. He painted from life too. His skin tones came from a stipple of tiny red dots, sometimes described as measles. Poor eyesight in the later 1740s made him hand his business to James Deacon.

Pierre-Antoine Baudouin married the younger daughter of François Boucher in 1758. He had been Boucher's pupil and imitator, and Boucher's influence helped get him elected an Academician in 1763 as a miniature painter. For the occasion he presented a drawing of Hyperides pleading the cause of Phryne before the Areopagus, now in the Louvre. He made idyllic and erotic subjects in watercolours and crayons and rarely painted in oils. His father Michel was an engraver.

Juan Bautista Martínez del Mazo imitated his father-in-law Velázquez more closely than any other follower. He married Velázquez's only surviving daughter, Francisca, in 1633. Nobody knows where he trained, though he must have been in Velázquez's workshop before the wedding. Sources disagree on whether he was born in Cuenca or Madrid. His most celebrated work is the View of Saragossa, which shows he was a master of landscape as well as portraits.

Louis Meijer is best known for seascapes. Born in Amsterdam, he studied with George Pieter Westenberg and Jan Willem Pieneman and went through all the classes of the Royal Academy of Art there. He first turned to sea painting in Deventer, after a steamship was wrecked. Matthijs Maris was his pupil from 1854. Meijer lived in Paris from 1841 and then in The Hague, and he died in Utrecht at 57.

Maksymilian Gierymski took part in the January Uprising at seventeen. He studied at the Warsaw Drawing School and then won a government scholarship in 1867 to the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich. There he became one of the leading painters of the Munich realist school, first known for battle paintings and later for landscapes, especially of southern Poland. He was successful in western Europe but never gained approval or popularity in Poland, although he sent paintings to Warsaw exhibitions from 1868. He died in 1874, and his younger brother Aleksander was a painter too.

Gillis van Coninxloo spent the last 20 years of his life abroad, first in Germany and then in the Dutch Republic. His father died when he was only about 10 months old. His mother kept the family going by selling paintings in Antwerp and in cities in Brabant and Flanders. His aunt was married to the prominent artist Pieter Coecke van Aelst. Coninxloo helped shape northern landscape art around the turn of the 17th century, especially with his forest landscapes.

Simon van der Does painted Italianate landscapes in the manner of his father, Jacob, who taught him. According to Houbraken, he spent one year in England in his youth and could paint portraits in the style of Caspar Netscher. He was married but barely made ends meet. After his wife and father died, he was too depressed to paint and stayed three years in the Gasthuis of The Hague. Later he moved to Brussels and then to Antwerp. He taught the future art historian Johan van Gool.

Andries Both drowned in a canal in Venice as he returned from festivities. Born in Utrecht, the son of a glass painter, he studied under Abraham Bloemaert. In Rome he joined the bamboccianti, the Dutch and Flemish painters who showed the everyday life of the lower classes. His presence there is documented from 1635 to 1641. He first shared a studio with a fellow Utrecht painter, Jan van Causteren. His brother Jan joined him later.

Christoph Amberger's main work was the history of Joseph in twelve pictures. His father was a stonemason. Amberger was a disciple of Hans Holbein and painted portraits in a similar style, as well as frescoes. He visited Augsburg every year, when men of power gathered and commissions came up. Among his sitters were Jakob Fugger, Konrad Peutinger, Georg von Frundsberg and Emperor Charles V. He travelled to northern Italy and Venice between 1525 and 1527.

Jean-Jacques Champin got his first name from Rousseau, whom his father admired. The father, Pierre, was an engraver and landscape painter, and also mayor of Sceaux. Besides his father, Champin studied with Félix Storelli and Jacques Auguste Regnier, and with Regnier he later made books of picturesque views of castles and the homes of famous people around Paris. In 1815 he moved to Paris and took up the new process of lithography. His first print showed the church in Sceaux. He travelled to the Chartreuse Mountains, the Pyrénées and Italy for his historical landscapes.

Adolf Ulrik Wertmüller's Danaë receiving Jupiter in a Shower of Gold was controversial as one of the earliest female nude paintings shown in America. Born in Stockholm, he moved to Paris in 1772 to study under his cousin Alexander Roslin and under Joseph-Marie Vien. Gustav III of Sweden commissioned him to paint Marie Antoinette, and the portrait is now in the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm. He emigrated to the United States in 1794 and painted George Washington among others. He was called back to Sweden but returned to Philadelphia in 1800.

Alexis Simon Belle painted portraits of the French and Jacobite nobility. Born in Paris, he studied first with his father Jean-Baptiste, also a painter, and then in the studio of François de Troy, court painter to the exiled James II at Saint-Germain-en-Laye. He began producing work at Saint-Germain between 1698 and 1701. Those were years of peace between France and Britain. His style followed Troy, Hyacinthe Rigaud and Nicolas de Largillière. Jacques Aved was his pupil.

Francisco Rizi's father was an Italian painter from Ancona who came to Spain in 1583 to do decorative work at El Escorial. Francisco began his apprenticeship in that workshop and then studied with Vicente Carducho. His brother Juan became a painter too. Carducho's influence got him contacts at the Royal Court in 1634. In the 1640s he became one of the earliest painters in Spain to adopt the Baroque style, as in a large altarpiece for the Capuchins that recalls Rubens or Van Dyck.

Hans Witdoeck belonged to the last generation of reproductive engravers who worked for Rubens' workshop. He trained with Lucas Vorsterman, Rubens' primary engraver, but broke the three-year contract after two years at his father's urging. He then trained for two years with the painter Cornelis Schut, who introduced him to painting, and afterwards with Rubens himself, where he learned to engrave large plates. After Rubens died in 1640, Witdoeck worked mainly as an art dealer. He married in 1642, and since no records follow, he is presumed to have died soon after.

Joseph Van Lerius painted mythological and biblical scenes as well as portraits and genre pictures, and much of his work is didactic. Born near Antwerp, he studied under Gustave Wappers. After a study trip through Germany and Italy in 1852, he became a painting instructor at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts of Antwerp. Among his students was Lawrence Alma-Tadema, along with Aloïs Boudry and Gerard Portielje. He died in Mechelen in 1876, where he had gone for treatment of meningitis.

Ludovico Marchetti learned painting in the studio of Mariano Fortuny, the Spanish painter who lived in Rome in the 1870s. In 1878, aged twenty-five, he moved to France and stayed there for the rest of his life. He exhibited at the Salon and won a bronze medal in 1889, and he later showed in Munich and Berlin, where he gained a sizeable following. He specialised in historical period pieces from the 16th to 18th centuries, made for petit-bourgeois taste. His favourite subjects were the cavaliers, troubadours and courtiers of the 18th century in richly coloured clothes.

Eduard Hallberger started his own publishing firm in Stuttgart during the revolutions, with an emphasis on youth and folk literature. He was the son of a publisher and bookseller and served his apprenticeship in his father's company before working for publishers in Potsdam and Berlin. In 1853 he created a family magazine that reached a circulation of 150,000 copies. With Friedrich Wilhelm Hackländer and Edmund Zoller he then founded the illustrated news magazine Über Land und Meer, which ran until 1923. For its illustrations he built one of the largest xylographic companies in Germany.

William James Bennett was sent to Egypt in 1805 at the age of eighteen, in an appointment attached to the army's medical staff, and he sketched views there and in Malta. Born in London, he studied at the Royal Academy Schools as a pupil of Westall. On a second posting to the Mediterranean he visited several parts of Italy and took leave to see Florence and Rome. He went to the United States around 1826. In 1828 he became a member of the National Academy of Design in New York, where he exhibited watercolour landscapes, seascapes and engravings.

Alida Withoos is best known for her botanical watercolours made for two large collaborative projects, Agnes Block's florilegium and the Moninckx Atlas. Her father, Matthias Withoos, taught her still lifes and botanical illustration, along with her siblings. Women were excluded from universities and guilds then, but daughters of artistic families could train in a studio. She was born in Amersfoort, and the family moved to Hoorn in 1672 because French troops invaded Utrecht. In 1701 she married the fijnschilder Andries Cornelisz van Dalen.

Christian Ludwig von Hagedorn studied law at Altdorf, but his letters show he was already interested in art. He entered the diplomatic service in 1737 as a legation secretary and rose to legation counselor. At the German courts where he was posted he visited the art collections, and over fifteen years of service he built up a substantial collection of his own. He wrote to critics such as Johann Joachim Winckelmann, Johann Georg Sulzer and Salomon Gessner. His elder brother Friedrich was a well known poet. Hagedorn also engraved as an amateur.

Georg Scholz joined the Communist Party of Germany in 1919, and his work of the next few years is harshly critical of the social and economic order in postwar Germany. Industrial Farmers of 1920 shows a Bible-clutching farmer with money erupting from his forehead, seated next to his monstrous wife, who cradles a piglet. Their son, with his head open at the top to show it is empty, is torturing a frog. Scholz studied at the Karlsruhe Academy under Hans Thoma and Wilhelm Trübner. Later he studied in Berlin under Lovis Corinth.

Jacob van Walscapelle was baptized Jacobus Cruydenier. He was a pupil of Cornelis Kick from 1664 to 1667 and painted fruit and flower still lifes in the manner of Jan Davidsz de Heem. Many of his works have been confused with Kick's. According to Houbraken, the two painted flowers from nature in Kick's garden outside the St Anthony's gate in Amsterdam. When Kick decided to move to Loenen, Walscapelle left his service and went back to Amsterdam, where he took up another profession. He influenced the painter Michel Nicolas Micheux.

Jacques Blanchard was raised and taught by his uncle, the painter Nicolas Baullery. Very little is known of his early development, despite his polished and prolific output as a religious and decorative painter. By 1618 he had travelled to Lyon to work in the studio of Horace le Blanc, and when Le Blanc left for Paris in 1623, Blanchard finished a number of the works he left behind. His travels in Italy began in 1624. His brother Jean-Baptiste and his son Gabriel were painters too.

John Hesselius painted portraits of wealthy politicians and planters in colonial Maryland, and the work made him a wealthy man too. He was the son of the Swedish-born portraitist Gustavus Hesselius and was probably born in Philadelphia, where his father kept a house for clients. A fire at Gloria Dei Church in 1740 would have destroyed any record of his birth. In 1750 his father received two letters from him, written near Williamsburg. He probably left Philadelphia to escape competition from better-known artists there. He died in 1778.

José Moreno Carbonero is considered one of the last great history painters of the 19th century. A prominent member of the Málaga School, he was also a celebrated portrait painter who enjoyed the patronage of Madrid's high society. He painted genre scenes and some landscapes and still lifes too. He won awards in Paris, Budapest and Berlin, and he took a medal at the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893. The Prado holds an important collection of his work, including The Prince Don Carlos of Viana from 1881.

Masaccio was born Tommaso di Ser Giovanni di Simone, and his nickname means clumsy or messy Tom. It may have been created to tell him apart from his principal collaborator, also named Maso, who came to be known as Masolino. His career was brief, since he died in the summer of 1428. Even so, he is considered to have started the Early Italian Renaissance in painting with his works of the mid and late 1420s. He was one of the first to use linear perspective. Vasari thought him the best painter of his generation for his skill at imitating nature.

Oscar Gustave Rejlander worked with Charles Darwin on The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, and that collaboration secured him a place in the history of behavioural science. He was born in Stockholm, the son of a stonemason and army officer, and the family later moved to Rauma in Finland. In the 1830s he relocated to England. He set up as a portraitist in Wolverhampton, probably around 1846. In the early 1850s he learned the wet-collodion and waxed-paper processes at great speed with Nicholas Henneman in London. He was an expert in photomontage.

A book of George Fiske's photographs helped draw the young Ansel Adams to Yosemite. His Aunt Mary gave him a copy of the book by James Hutchings when he was sick, and in 1916 his parents took him on a vacation there. Fiske was born in Amherst, New Hampshire, and moved west with his brother to San Francisco, where he apprenticed under Charles L. Weed and worked with Carleton Watkins. In 1879 he and his wife moved to Yosemite. Most of his negatives were destroyed when his house burned in 1904.

Natale Schiavoni was born in Chioggia near Venice, and Frederick Mason Perkins claimed he was a distant descendant of the Renaissance painter Andrea Schiavone. He trained in Venice with Francesco Maggiotto and later came under the influence of Neoclassicism. In 1810 he moved to Milan, where he painted Eugène de Beauharnais and the royal family. In 1816 the Austrian emperor invited him to Vienna to be the official portraitist of the court. He returned to Venice in 1821 and became professor at the Academy of Fine Arts.

William Alfred Delamotte showed such skill at drawing so early that King George III became his patron. He was the son of a French refugee, exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1793 and enrolled at the Royal Academy Schools the next year as a student of Benjamin West. He moved to Oxford and drew its buildings in many sketches, and Orlando Jewitt of Headington made woodcuts from many of them. In 1803 he became drawing-master at the new Royal Military College, Sandhurst. He held the post for forty years.

William Havell was one of fourteen children, born in Reading to Luke Havell, a drawing master who also kept a small shop to eke out his narrow means. Luke knew the money troubles an artist's life could bring and at first discouraged his son. William's talent won him over, and he funded a sketching trip to Wales. In 1804 William sent his first contribution to the Royal Academy, a view of Carnarvon Castle and another of the valley of Nant Ffrancon. The same year he became a founding member of the Society of Painters in Watercolours.

Anton Francesco Lucini said he spent 12 years and used 5,000 pounds of copper making the plates for Sir Robert Dudley's book of sea charts, Dell'Arcano del Mare. It was published in Florence in 1646 and 1647. The elegant Baroque look of Dudley's charts is credited to his engraving. Lucini was born in Florence and studied etching under Stefano della Bella and Jacques Callot, who had lived in Florence and strongly influenced local printmakers. Earlier he made a series of engravings of the Turkish siege of Malta, published in Bologna.

The eldest son of Maurice Baquoy, Jean Charles Baquoy was born and died in Paris. He engraved book-plates after designs by Eisen, Gravelot, Moreau and others. Among them is a set of vignettes for the French translation of Ovid's Metamorphoses, published by Basan, which are executed in a finished style. He also made a set of plates after Jean-Baptiste Oudry for the Fables of La Fontaine, as well as engravings after Boucher, Watteau, J. Vernet and Wouwerman.

Oskar Kallis devoted his short career mostly to illustrating Kalevipoeg, the Estonian national epic, and made about 40 works for it. The Finnish painter Akseli Gallen-Kallela influenced him strongly. He studied in Ants Laikmaa's studio and took design at the Estonian Artist Society. In 1917 he helped found the artistic association Vikerla. He also designed furniture and textiles in an ethnographic style. He died of tuberculosis in Crimea in 1918.

Wenzel Jamnitzer was the best known German goldsmith of his era and court goldsmith to a succession of emperors, including Charles V, Ferdinand I, Maximilian II and Rudolf II. Born in Vienna into a Moravian German family that had produced works for more than 160 years, he was trained by his father Hans the Elder, along with his brother Albrecht. In 1534 he settled in Nuremberg. He made vases and jewelry boxes with great skill, and he probably invented an embossing machine. His son Hans and grandson Christof continued the business.

Willem Jacob Herreyns came from a family of artists. His great-grandfather and grandfather were both painters called Jacob Herreyns, his father was a painter and decorator, and his uncle Daniel was a sculptor. They gave him his first training, and he then studied at the Academy of Antwerp, where Balthasar Beschey was one of his teachers. He won the first prize for painting from life in 1764. A year later he became one of the academy's six director-teachers. He is regarded as the last follower of Rubens.

Carl Johan Fahlcrantz grew up as a vicar's son in Dalarna and went to Stockholm in 1791 to apprentice as a decorative painter at the Royal Dramatic Theatre. After a year he became a student of Emanuel Limnell and lived with his family until around 1800. He also got guidance from Elias Martin and studied landscape painting with Louis Belanger, who had come from France in 1798. Soon he received numerous orders for landscapes and vedute. His brothers were the sculptor Axel Magnus and the theologian Christian Eric.

Luis Mora was born in Montevideo to the Catalan sculptor Domingo Mora and a French mother, Laura Gaillard, whose two sisters married into the Bacardi rum family. Mora stayed close to the Bacardis all his life. His younger brother Jo became a noted sculptor and author in California. The family left Uruguay during an insurgency in 1877. Mora worked in watercolor, oils and tempera, and he made etchings and monotypes too. He was also a popular art instructor.

Samuel Ireland is best known as the chief victim of the Shakespeare forgeries made by his son William Henry Ireland. He began life as a weaver in Spitalfields, then dealt in prints and drawings and taught himself drawing, etching and engraving. He won a medal from the Society of Arts in 1760. In 1784 he exhibited at the Royal Academy for the first and apparently only time, with a view of Oxford. He etched many plates after John Hamilton Mortimer and Hogarth. The British Museum print room holds his etched portraits of General Oglethorpe and Thomas Inglefield.
